questions.prompt: What does the disappearing-door experiment mainly show?
choices: People always prefer the newest option.
People can overprotect options that are about to disappear even when those options are not best.
People never value flexibility.

explanation.gentle: The experiment shows that threatened options can attract effort simply because losing them feels painful.
explanation.direct: Imminent closure makes weak doors feel worth preserving.
explanation.competitive: Vanishing doors get a fake premium.

questions.prompt: Why do participants keep revisiting weak doors in Ariely's setup?
choices: Because the weak doors suddenly become more rewarding.
Because closure itself starts to feel costly.
Because they forget which door pays best.

explanation.gentle: The fear of losing the option becomes part of the decision.
explanation.direct: People respond to threatened loss, not just to payoff.
explanation.competitive: They are defending against closure more than chasing value.

questions.prompt: What hidden cost often comes with keeping many options open?
choices: Less focus and more switching.
Automatic higher quality choices.
A stronger sense of commitment.

explanation.gentle: Open doors can divide attention and make progress weaker.
explanation.direct: Option maintenance creates switching costs and diluted performance.
explanation.competitive: The hallway of backups raids the main road.

questions.prompt: What is Ariely criticizing in this chapter?
choices: All forms of flexibility.
Fear-driven option-hoarding.
Trying new things early.

explanation.gentle: The chapter targets preserving weak alternatives only because closure feels bad.
explanation.direct: Ariely is critiquing anxious preservation, not all optionality.
explanation.competitive: The problem is worshipping every maybe.

questions.prompt: Why is this chapter not just generic advice about commitment?
choices: Because it isolates a specific distortion around threatened loss of options.
Because it says commitment is always easy.
Because it rejects experimentation altogether.

explanation.gentle: Ariely is showing how closure anxiety changes behavior, not merely praising decisiveness.
explanation.direct: The mechanism is loss aversion around vanishing possibilities.
explanation.competitive: This is a loss problem wearing the clothes of flexibility.

questions.prompt: What practical move best fits the chapter's advice?
choices: Keep every possible backup alive just in case.
Close low-value doors that no longer earn their maintenance cost.
Avoid making choices until every risk is gone.

explanation.gentle: Strategic closure helps protect focus for the paths that still matter.
explanation.direct: Weak options should not stay open by default.
explanation.competitive: Make doors earn their oxygen or shut them.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter apply beyond literal doors in an experiment?
choices: It applies to projects, roles, plans, and schedules that people keep half-open.
It applies only to casino-style games.
It applies only when money is directly involved.

explanation.gentle: Many real-life choices involve maintaining options that consume time and attention.
explanation.direct: The same pattern appears in work, school, and personal commitments.
explanation.competitive: Any maybe can turn into a disappearing door if loss starts doing the thinking.

questions.prompt: What limit does Ariely place on the chapter's claim?
choices: He says all optionality is irrational.
He says some flexibility is useful, but weak options should not survive on fear alone.
He says commitment should replace every form of exploration.

explanation.gentle: The chapter allows for real uncertainty and useful backups.
explanation.direct: The issue is fear-driven maintenance, not all flexibility.
explanation.competitive: Real backups can stay. Panic doors should not.

questions.prompt: What resource is most visibly drained when too many options remain open?
choices: Attention
Luck
Memory alone

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps showing how focus gets fragmented by too many maintained options.
explanation.direct: Attention is the main currency lost to option-hoarding.
explanation.competitive: The calendar and focus pay the bill.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 8 set up the move into expectations in Chapter 9?
choices: It shows how a frame can change behavior before value is fully checked.
It proves that expectations do not matter.
It says perception and choice are completely separate.

explanation.gentle: The chapter prepares the next move by showing that conditions around a choice can shape behavior early.
explanation.direct: It primes the idea that a frame can distort judgment before evidence is fully weighed.
explanation.competitive: First vanishing doors bend attention, then expectations bend experience.
